facts.statement: Indosinosuchus lived in what is now Thailand during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus is a genus of teleosaurid crocodyliform that lived during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous in what is now Thailand.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis is the only named teleosaurid genus known from a freshwater environment, whereas most other members of the group are marine.
facts.quote: It is unique among teleosauroids as the type species is the only named genus known from a freshwater environment, while most other members including I. peninsularensis are marine.

facts.statement: Most Indosinosuchus fossils come from a single site interpreted as a mass death event, possibly caused by drought or flash floods.
facts.quote: Most known specimens of this genus were recovered from a single locality, which has been interpreted as a mass death site, possibly caused by a drought or flash flood.

facts.statement: By 2019, ten individuals of Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis were known from the Phu Noi locality in the Phu Kradung Formation.
facts.quote: By 2019, when Martin and colleagues named Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis, ten individuals known from skull remains and various assorted postcranial fossils were known from the Phu Kradung Formation, all collected from Phu Noi.

facts.statement: Specimen PRC-11, a complete skull and mandible, was designated the holotype for Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
facts.quote: Of the material, specimen PRC-11 (a complete skull and mandible) was chosen as the holotype.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis has four teeth per premaxilla, thirty teeth per maxilla, and thirty-one teeth per dentary.
facts.quote: Four teeth are situated in each premaxilla of I. potamosiamensis, organized into two closely spaced pairs, followed by 30 teeth in either of the only faintly ornamented maxillae and opposed by 31 dentary teeth.

facts.statement: All teeth of Indosinosuchus are slender, conical, and have curved crowns.
facts.quote: All teeth are slender and conical in shape with a curved crown.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus has osteoderms that are wider than long on the trunk and longer than wide on the tail, all featuring a front-to-back keel.
facts.quote: The osteoderm armor of Indosinosuchus follows the patterns typical for teleosaurs, with wider than long osteoderms in the trunk region and longer than wide, subrectangular osteoderms on the tail, all of which preserve a keel that runs from the front to the back.

facts.statement: Underside osteoderms of Indosinosuchus are longer than wide, lack a keel, and form a flat surface.
facts.quote: The osteoderm on the underside of the body are also longer than wide, but lack the keel and subsequently form a flat surface.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus is classified in the family Teleosauridae, though its robust skull resembles members of Machimosauridae.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus is placed in the family Teleosauridae, but has a relatively robust skull that bears resemblance to members of the Machimosauridae.

facts.statement: In 2020, Johnson, Young, and Brusatte examined specimen PRC-239, which was previously referred to Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
facts.quote: In their 2020 revision of teleosauroids, Johnson, Young and Brusatte also examined specimen PRC-239, which was among the various specimen referred to I. potamosiamensis.

facts.statement: A 2026 study by Lauprasert and colleagues questioned the validity of Indosinosuchus kalasinensis after examining material from Ban Nam Pun.
facts.quote: However, this conclusion was eventually questioned in a 2026 study by Komsorn Lauprasert and colleagues as they described the teleosauroid material from Ban Nam Pun.

facts.statement: The premaxillae of Indosinosuchus form a snout tip that expands moderately to the side, a trait that varies among teleosaurs.
facts.quote: The tip of the snout, formed by the premaxillae, expands moderately to the side, which is a trait that varies between teleosaurs.

facts.statement: The raised rims of the circular eye sockets give Indosinosuchus a telescopic appearance similar to modern gharials.
facts.quote: The rims of the circular eye sockets are raised, giving them a somewhat telescopic appearance similar to modern gharials.

facts.statement: Unlike gharials, the eyes of Indosinosuchus were directed slightly towards the sides as well as upwards.
facts.quote: Unlike gharials however, in which the eyes are directed purely upwards, the eyes of Indosinosuchus would be directed a little towards the sides as well.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus has a humerus to femur ratio of 0.63, consistent with its relatives.
facts.quote: Here too Indosinosuchus follows what is seen in its relatives, with a humerus to femur ratio of 0.63.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus was initially described by Martin and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: In the initial description by Martin and colleagues in 2019, Indosinosuchus was recovered as a close relative of the robust teleosauroid Machimosaurus hugii

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis suggests I. kalasinensis is the most basal member of Teleosauridae, while I. potamosinensis is more derived.
facts.quote: In the most parsimonious tree using the extended implied weights method, I. kalasinensis was found to be the basalmost member of Teleosauridae while I. potamosinensis was notably more derived

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the lack of recovered relationships between Indosinosuchus species in some studies may be due to insufficient fossil material and poor preservation of the postcranial skeleton.
facts.quote: Part of the reason for this lack of a recovered relationship could be the lack of material for I. kalasinensis and the fact that the two species do not preserve as much of the postcranial skeleton as their relatives

facts.statement: I. potamosiamensis has the highest posterior mechanical advantage of any known teleosaur, indicating the greatest maximum force along its tooth row.
facts.quote: The posterior mechanical advantage (pMa) of I. potamosiamensis, which describes the overall maximum force along the toothrow, is the single highest among all teleosaurs

facts.statement: I. potamosiamensis had the highest jaw-opening speed among teleosaurs, whereas I. kalasinensis had a lower opening mechanical advantage, suggesting a faster bite.
facts.quote: The former was recovered as having an expectedly high opening mechanical advantage, the highest among teleosaurs, while the specimen attributed to I. kalasinensis had a relatively low oMa, giving it a much faster bite than

facts.statement: It is debated whether the differences in bite mechanics between I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis represent distinct ecological niches or are merely artifacts of post-mortem skull distortion.
facts.quote: This was initially interpreted as two contemporary species having filled different ecological niches, but other research has argued that the two forms were not distinst and that the differences were merely a matter of post-mortem distortion of the skull

facts.statement: The Phu Noi locality where I. potamosiamensis fossils were found represents an oxbow lake or abandoned river channel.
facts.quote: The Phu Noi locality has been interpreted as representing an oxbow lake or the abandoned channel of one of the many meandering rivers of the region

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the age of the Phu Kradung Formation, with faunal evidence suggesting the Late Jurassic while zircon and palynological data suggest the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: On the one hand, the general fauna of the formation better matches the Late Jurassic while dating using zircons and palynological data both point towards the Early Cretaceous

facts.statement: A hypothesis suggests the formation straddles the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary, marking the replacement of freshwater teleosaurs by goniopholids and pholidosaurids in the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: This would be congruent with the hypothesis that freshwater teleosaurs, which were dominant in the lower parts of the formation were replaced by goniopholids and pholidosaurids such as Chalawan thailandicus during the Cretaceous

facts.statement: Indosuchus peninsularensis dates to the late-Middle to early-Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: This species was furthermore older, dating to the late-Middle to early–Late Jurassic

facts.statement: Ten Indosinosuchus specimens ranging from juveniles to fully mature adults were discovered at Phu Noi.
facts.quote: The discovery of 10 Indosinosuchus specimen at Phu Noi, which cover different ages from juvenile to full mature

facts.statement: One nearly complete specimen with an articulated vertebral column may have been preserved after the animal floated on water, lost its head, and was rapidly buried.
facts.quote: One specimen in particular, a nearly complete and still articulated vertebral column, could have been preserved when the bloated corpse of the animal floated on the water surface and lost its head

facts.statement: Marks from dermestid beetles on fossils suggest the carcasses dried out for at least 8 weeks, indicating preservation during a dry season.
facts.quote: This is supported by marks left from the activity of dermestid beetles on some of the fossils, which would only be active in the dry season and require at least 8 weeks of dry conditions for their larvae to fully develop

facts.statement: It is debated whether the animals died in a flash flood or during a drought, with decomposition occurring as waters receded.
facts.quote: Alternatively, the animals may have died in a flash flood, their decomposition beginning while the waters were still receding but eventually leaving the carcasses stranded on dry land
